session_roles.display_text:
Why: Learn where opponents naturally retreat so pressure can steer instead of chase.
- Pressure Route Scan: 10 minutes, tactical review only. No physical load.
  Step 1: Identify the opponent's preferred retreat direction.
  Step 2: Choose the direction you should step to cut that route.
  Step 3: Identify the cue that tells you pressure should start.
  Step 4: Choose the area of the ring you want to trap them in.
  Intent: Guide the opponent toward the space you want.
  Focus: Watch the first direction they choose when space disappears.
  Reset: If you start following, pause and rebuild the angle.
  Anchor: Cut the ring, do not chase it.
  Purpose: Early-camp pressure route study for a pressure fighter.
  Progress: Use one technical round to steer toward the chosen trap instead of following.
Review the last clean technical work. Write three cues only: one entry, one defensive reset, one composure cue.

session_roles.display_text:
Why: Build a repeatable way into the pocket without walking onto clean shots.
- Safe Entry Builder: 10 minutes, tactical review only. No physical load.
  Step 1: Choose the setup that hides your forward step.
  Step 2: Choose the guard position you need while crossing range.
  Step 3: Choose the first punch that establishes the pocket.
  Step 4: Define where your head should finish after the entry.
  Intent: Arrive protected before trying to win the exchange.
  Focus: Watch what the opponent throws as someone closes distance.
  Reset: If the entry is naked, leave and rebuild the setup.
  Anchor: Earn the pocket.
  Purpose: Early-camp entry quality for a pressure fighter.
  Progress: Rehearse the same setup and head position before adding longer combinations.
Nasal breathing if comfortable. Use a 4 second inhale and 6 second exhale. Finish calmer than you started.

Why: Rehearse taking space and finishing exchanges in position rather than chasing.
- Tactical Picture: 12 minutes, optional mental rehearsal. No physical load.
  Step 1: Visualise them giving ground.
  Step 2: See yourself taking space without following them blindly.
  Step 3: Cut their preferred exit, enter behind your trained setup and finish the exchange balanced.
  Step 4: Run it again with them changing direction and adjust instead of chasing.
  Cue: Take the space, do not chase it.

Why: Recognise how the opponent reacts to pressure before committing to the next attack.
- Read → React: 12 minutes, optional mental rehearsal. No physical load.
  Step 1: Picture the opponent retreating straight, covering high or planting to counter.
  Step 2: Recognise the reaction before choosing your response.
  Step 3: Use only responses already trained in camp.
  Step 4: Finish each exchange balanced and reset your pressure.
  Cue: Read before you chase.

Why: Rehearse restarting pressure from position after being caught or escaped.
- Pressure → Reset: 12 minutes, optional mental rehearsal. No physical load.
  Step 1: Picture getting caught while entering.
  Step 2: Do not rush back in. Exhale, rebuild your stance and restart your pressure from position.
  Step 3: Then picture the opponent escaping your trap.
  Step 4: Reset the angle instead of chasing.
  Cue: Reset the angle, not the pace.

Why: Know what happens after the first punches so pocket exchanges stay planned rather than chaotic.
- Pocket Exchange Map: 10 minutes, tactical review only. No physical load.
  Step 1: Identify the opponent's most common pocket sequence.
  Step 2: Choose your answer to that sequence.
  Step 3: Choose the finishing shot that best fits the opening.
  Step 4: Decide whether that exchange should end with an exit or a smother.
  Intent: Win the second decision inside the pocket.
  Focus: Watch the opponent's response after the first two punches.
  Reset: If the exchange loses shape, smother or leave instead of trading blindly.
  Anchor: Know the next beat.
  Purpose: SPP pocket planning for a pressure fighter.
  Progress: Rehearse the chosen exchange ending, not just the opening combination.

Why: Find safe body attacks that reward pressure without making the entry predictable.
- Body Attack Opportunity: 10 minutes, tactical review only. No physical load.
  Step 1: Identify the clearest body opening the opponent gives away.
  Step 2: Choose the punch or feint that creates that opening.
  Step 3: Choose the body target you will attack.
  Step 4: Choose the head follow-up that punishes their reaction.
  Intent: Attack the body when the position earns it.
  Focus: Watch for high guards, separated elbows and upright posture.
  Reset: If the body line closes, go back upstairs rather than forcing it.
  Anchor: Open it before you take it.
  Purpose: SPP body-attack selection for a pressure fighter.
  Progress: Use the body attack only after the chosen setup appears in technical work.
Nasal breathing if comfortable. Use a 4 second inhale and 6 second exhale. Finish calmer than you started.

session_roles.display_text:
Why: Stop the opponent firing back immediately after your pressure combination lands.
- Smother and Reset: 10 minutes, tactical review only. No physical load.
  Step 1: Choose where your body should finish after the combination.
  Step 2: Choose your response if the opponent fires back immediately.
  Step 3: Define the smother or control position you can reach safely.
  Step 4: Choose the action that resets you for the next pressure sequence.
  Intent: Own the space after your combination as well as during it.
  Focus: Watch when the opponent begins their return fire.
  Reset: Close the return, then rebuild before attacking again.
  Anchor: Finish safe before restarting.
  Purpose: SPP post-combination control for a pressure fighter.
  Progress: Finish every rehearsed combination with the same smother-or-reset decision.

Why: Confirm controlled opening pressure without turning fight-night energy into a reckless start.
- First-Round Pressure Script: 8 minutes, tactical review only. No physical load.
  Step 1: Choose the opening pressure action you already trust.
  Step 2: Choose the first ring cut you want to establish.
  Step 3: Choose the first familiar combination you will show.
  Step 4: Write one reset cue that prevents chasing.
  Intent: Take space calmly before increasing the exchange rate.
  Focus: Use only the pressure actions already rehearsed in camp.
  Reset: If you rush, rebuild the ring cut before throwing again.
  Anchor: Close calmly.
  Purpose: Fight-week opening script for a pressure fighter.
  Progress: Rehearse the script once at low intensity and keep it unchanged.

Why: Reduce your pressure plan to one familiar instruction that keeps aggression organised.
- Final Pressure Cue: 6 minutes, tactical review only. No physical load.
  Step 1: Review one successful pressure sequence from camp.
  Step 2: Choose the behaviour that made the pressure work.
  Step 3: Turn it into one cue of no more than six words.
  Intent: Carry controlled forward pressure into the fight.
  Focus: Keep the cue tied to positioning, not emotion.
  Reset: Return to the same cue whenever the pace becomes messy.
  Anchor: Position before volume.
  Purpose: Final taper compression for a pressure fighter.
  Progress: Use the same cue in the final light rehearsal and do not add another.

session_roles.display_text:
Why: Confirm a familiar opening sequence without adding new decisions during taper.
- Familiar Round-One Rehearsal: 7 minutes, tactical review only. No physical load.
  Step 1: Choose the first familiar action you will show.
  Step 2: Choose the response you already trust if the opponent disrupts it.
  Step 3: Choose the position you want after the opening exchange.
  Step 4: Say the sequence once in plain language.
  Intent: Start with what has already worked in camp.
  Focus: Use only confirmed actions and responses.
  Reset: If the opening changes, return to the safest familiar action.
  Anchor: Familiar first.
  Purpose: General fight-week opening rehearsal.
  Progress: Rehearse the sequence once at low intensity, then stop analysing it.
